summary: Describes the structure and identification of management information for TCP/IP-based internets, the rules for how managed items are named and defined. It is a re-release of RFC 1065 with a changed status section and typo fixes. It is an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Before devices can report on themselves, everyone needs to agree on how things are named. This is the naming system.

questions: what is the structure of management information
what is the 1.3.6.1 object identifier prefix
what are snmp counter and gauge types
subtitle: The naming scheme and building blocks that every SNMP-managed device uses to describe what it can report.

tldr.problem: To manage devices from many vendors, everyone must agree on how each managed item is named, what kind of value it holds and how its definition is written down.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1155 names every managed object with an OBJECT IDENTIFIER on a global tree rooted at the internet prefix 1.3.6.1, limits the ASN.1 types that may be used, and defines a standard OBJECT-TYPE format for describing objects.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that re-releases RFC 1065 with a changed status section and typo fixes, and it leaves the actual objects to the MIB memo and the protocol to the SNMP memo.

today: RFC 1155 is an Internet Standard and, according to the metadata for this page, it has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 1065, whose technical content it carries unchanged.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1155 describes the common structures and identification scheme used to define management information for TCP/IP-based internets. It gives an object information model and a set of generic types, and writes them down formally in Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1).

The memo is mostly about organizational concerns and administrative policy. It does not say which objects are managed and it does not say which protocol manages them. Those jobs belong to two companion memos: RFC 1156 for the Management Information Base (MIB) and RFC 1157 for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

Its two goals are simplicity and extensibility. The authors say that understanding of internet management was not yet complete, so a simple SMI puts the fewest constraints on future approaches, and an extensible one leaves the most room for experiments. It differs from an earlier IETF working note in one big way: that note focused entirely on OSI-style management and so was not suitable for SNMP.
sections.eli5: This memo does not say what to measure or how to ask. It only says how things get their names and what kinds of values they can have, so the other memos can build on it.

sections.title: Naming Objects with OBJECT IDENTIFIERs
sections.content:
Every object type has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is a unique OBJECT IDENTIFIER: a sequence of integers that walks down a global tree. Each node has a label made of a short text description and an integer, and control over the meaning of nodes can be handed down as you go deeper.

Under the unlabeled root sit ccitt(0), iso(1) and joint-iso-ccitt(2). Following iso, org(3) and dod(6), the memo assumes the Department of Defense will give the Internet community a node, administered by the Internet Activities Board: internet ::= { iso org(3) dod(6) 1 }, which is the prefix 1.3.6.1.

Four subtrees start under internet:

  • directory(1): reserved for a future memo on using the OSI Directory in the Internet.
  • mgmt(2): objects defined in IAB-approved documents. The first Internet-standard MIB would be management document number 1, so it uses { mgmt 1 }, or 1.3.6.1.2.1.
  • experimental(3): objects used in Internet experiments. An experimenter given number 17 would use 1.3.6.1.3.17.
  • private(4): objects defined unilaterally. It holds enterprises(1), where vendors can register models of their products.

The IAB delegates administration of mgmt, experimental and private to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. The memo's own example is a made-up company numbered 1.3.6.1.4.1.42 registering a product at 1.3.6.1.4.1.42.1.1.
sections.eli5: Imagine a giant family tree where every branch has a number. Each thing gets its address by listing the branch numbers from the top, like 1.3.6.1. Different people look after different branches.

sections.title: Allowed Syntax and Defined Types
sections.content:
To keep things simple, the memo allows only part of ASN.1. The permitted primitive types are INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER and NULL. If an enumerated INTEGER is used, the value 0 must not appear among its named numbers.

The constructor type SEQUENCE is allowed only to make lists (a fixed set of primitive fields, always present) or tables (SEQUENCE OF an entry that is a list).

The memo also defines application-wide types:

  • NetworkAddress: a choice among protocol families; only the Internet family is present.
  • IpAddress: a 32-bit internet address, an OCTET STRING of length 4 in network byte order.
  • Counter: a non-negative integer that only increases and wraps to zero after its maximum of 4294967295.
  • Gauge: a non-negative integer that can go up or down but latches at the maximum of 4294967295.
  • TimeTicks: a count in hundredths of a second since an epoch named in each object's description.
  • Opaque: an arbitrary ASN.1 value encoded to octets and then wrapped again as an OCTET STRING. An implementation only has to accept and recognize such data, not unwrap it.

Values are carried using the ASN.1 basic encoding rules.
sections.eli5: The memo gives you a small box of building blocks: whole numbers, text, addresses, counters that go up, and gauges that go up and down like a thermometer. You may only build with those blocks.

sections.title: Defining Managed Objects
sections.content:
The memo does not define MIB objects, but it fixes how others must write them. An object type definition has five fields: OBJECT (a textual OBJECT DESCRIPTOR and its OBJECT IDENTIFIER), Syntax, Definition, Access (read-only, read-write, write-only or not-accessible) and Status (mandatory, optional or obsolete).

No object type in the Internet-standard MIB may use a sub-identifier of 0 in its name, because that value is reserved for future extensions. Each OBJECT DESCRIPTOR must be unique, mnemonic and printable.

The memo separates an object type, a declarative definition, from an object instance, a type bound to a value. A list type groups several simple types; a table is a SEQUENCE OF a list type. The worked example is an address translation table with entries holding atIndex, atPhysAddress and atNetAddress. How instances are referenced is left to each management protocol, which must also say which instances come back when a request matches more than one.

To help tools process definitions, an OBJECT-TYPE macro captures the SYNTAX, ACCESS and STATUS of an object formally.
sections.eli5: Every item on the list gets a little form: its name, what kind of answer it gives, what it means, whether you may change it, and whether it is still in use. Filling in the same form everywhere keeps things tidy.

sections.title: Extending the MIB Over Time
sections.content:
Every Internet-standard MIB document obsoletes all earlier ones. The tail of a name after { mgmt version-number } must stay the same between versions.

New versions may declare old object types obsolete (but not delete their names), append non-aggregate object types to a list type, or define entirely new object types. They may not change the meaning of an existing object without changing its name.

These rules let several MIB versions share the same tail names, which makes it much easier for an implementation to support more than one version. The price is that an agent might return an instance that is a superset of what the manager expected. Following the robustness principle, the manager should ignore the extra information. For control actions the rule is stricter: if an instance does not have the expected syntax, the action must fail. In every case the name of an object in a reply must be identical to the name requested.
sections.eli5: When the rulebook gets a new edition, old names keep their meaning. You can add new things, but you cannot quietly change what an old name means.

sections.title: Status and Security Notes
sections.content:
RFC 1155 is a re-release of RFC 1065 with a changed Status of this Memo and a few minor typographical corrections. The technical content is unchanged. It specifies a Standard Protocol with the status Recommended, and the Internet Activities Board recommends that all IP and TCP implementations be network manageable. That implies the Internet MIB (RFC 1156) and at least one of the management protocols SNMP (RFC 1157) or CMOT (RFC 1095).

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: This is a second printing of an earlier rulebook with small fixes. It says nothing about keeping secrets safe.
